To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the spatial representation of time is a robust phenomenon, which is not limited to the left/right axis, as it also involves a vertical dimension, and it is not limited to spatial attention as it extends to motor responses.
the past and future concepts are spatially coded in a mental time-line, and that this spatial representation is used to orient attention and prime responses in space.
the mere activation (without prediction) of past or future concepts orient spatial attention to left and right, respectively, and that these effects are independent of each other.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the nature of the space-time conceptual metaphor by showing that the mere activation in working memory of the past and future concepts can both prime a left or right motor response, respectively, and modulate the spatial attention system in a similar manner to central cues.
a new type of space-time conceptual metaphor that can be used as a tool for studying the neural bases of time perception.
how the conceptual system interacts with the sensorimotor system, and how this interaction is reflected at the behavioral and neural level.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
past and future concepts are both represented as spatial locations, and that this spatial representation is activated when the concepts are activated.
both the space-time conceptual metaphor and its underlying mechanism are supported.

the past-future space-time mapping is a bidirectional conceptual metaphor, with the past being associated with left space and the future with right space, and that these spatial representations are activated by temporal concepts.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the space-time conceptual metaphor is not only a spatial representation of time in the mind but also a motor representation of time in action.
the past and future are represented in a spatial mental time line and that this representation is used for the guidance of spatial attention.
time is represented in the brain in a similar way as space is.
The main takeaway from our work is that
time concepts have a direct impact on spatial attention, and this effect is independent from the motor response.

the space-time conceptual metaphor is not only a linguistic convention but also a cognitive mechanism that is automatically and unconsciously triggered by the mere activation of time concepts in working memory.
time is represented as space, and this representation is used to orient and direct our attention.
